text: Chapters 2 and 3 went deep on Azure Monitor and CloudWatch, each one real and useful on its own. The problem is that a team running production workloads in both clouds ends up with two separate consoles and two separate query languages during an incident that might involve either one. This lesson covers the tool teams reach for instead: Grafana, sitting on top of both as one unified visualization layer.

Grafana's core engine is cloud-agnostic, the same way Terraform's core doesn't know what Azure is — it only knows how to render panels from whatever data a data source plugin hands it. The cloud-specific logic lives entirely in that plugin. Grafana ships official data sources for both platforms, so a single dashboard can mix an Azure Monitor panel with a CloudWatch panel, rendered by the same engine in the same browser tab.

Data sources get set up once — connection details, default region or subscription — and every dashboard just references them. For a reproducible setup, that configuration can be provisioned from a YAML file instead of clicked together: one file defining an Azure Monitor data source and a CloudWatch data source, dropped into Grafana's provisioning folder, and both exist automatically the moment the instance starts, with the file itself living in source control.

Once both data sources exist, a panel simply points at the one it needs. A real dashboard JSON model can carry one panel titled for an AWS ALB's 5xx rate pointed at the cloudwatch data source, sitting right next to a panel for an Azure App Service's response time pointed at the Azure Monitor data source. The datasource field on each panel is the entire trick — it tells the engine which plugin to ask, and the engine itself never has to know AWS or Azure exist.

Template variables push the same dashboard further. A variable like dollar-sign region lets one dashboard definition serve dev, staging, and prod, or several AWS regions, without duplicating a single panel — every query that references it just re-evaluates when the dropdown at the top changes. It's the same reuse instinct a Terraform module applies to infrastructure, applied here to a dashboard instead.

That's the whole model: data sources carry the cloud-specific logic, panels pick a data source, and variables let one definition cover many environments. Next, these dashboards need alerts attached to them that actually reach the right person — without paging the whole team for every blip.
